content: Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) is a frequent and potentially life-threatening complication that can occur during childbirth. While there are several methods available to prevent PPH, there is a need for further advancements, particularly in identifying interventions that are safe, easy to administer, and cost-effective. Tranexamic acid (TA), an antifibrinolytic agent commonly used to prevent and treat bleeding, has been evaluated to determine its effectiveness and safety in preventing PPH. The objective of this study was to assess whether TA is effective and safe for preventing PPH when compared to placebo, no treatment, or uterotonic agents, either alone or in combination with uterotonics. A systematic search was conducted, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group’s Trials Register and reference lists of relevant studies. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) involving the use of TA during the third stage of labour or caesarean section (CS) to prevent PPH were included. Twelve trials involving 3285 healthy women at low risk of excessive bleeding were included in the analysis. These women underwent either elective CS (2453 participants across nine trials) or spontaneous vaginal birth (832 participants across three trials). All participants received routine prophylactic uterotonics as per local guidelines, in addition to either TA, placebo, or no intervention. The studies were assessed for risk of bias, with moderate risk noted for random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, and selective reporting, and low risk for incomplete data. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE system. The results showed that blood loss exceeding 400 mL or 500 mL, as well as blood loss greater than 1000 mL, was significantly less common in women who received TA compared to those who received placebo or no intervention. Specifically, the risk ratio (RR) for blood loss greater than 400 mL or 500 mL was 0.52 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.42 to 0.63) based on six trials involving 1398 women, and the RR for blood loss greater than 1000 mL was 0.40 (95% CI 0.23 to 0.71) based on six trials involving 2093 women. Both findings were supported by moderate-quality evidence. TA was particularly effective in reducing the incidence of blood loss greater than 1000 mL in women undergoing CS (RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.78, four trials, 1534 women). However, this effect was not observed in women who had vaginal births (RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.06 to 1.36, two trials, 559 women). Conversely, the effect of TA on blood loss greater than 500 mL or 400 mL was more pronounced in women who had vaginal births compared to those who underwent CS. The mean blood loss from delivery until two hours postpartum was lower in women who received TA compared to those who received placebo or no intervention. The mean difference (MD) was -77.79 mL (95% CI -97.95 to -57.64) based on five trials involving 1186 women. This reduction in blood loss was observed in both vaginal births and CS. Women who received TA required fewer additional medical interventions and blood transfusions compared to those who received placebo or no intervention. However, mild side effects such as nausea, vomiting, and dizziness were more commonly reported in women who received TA. These findings were supported by moderate-quality evidence. The effects of TA on maternal mortality, severe morbidity, and thromboembolic events remain uncertain due to low-quality evidence. In conclusion, TA, when used in addition to uterotonic medications, reduces postpartum blood loss and the need for blood transfusions in women at low risk of PPH following both vaginal birth and CS. However, there is insufficient evidence to draw definitive conclusions about serious side effects, although minor side effects appear to be more common with TA use. Further research is needed to evaluate the effects of TA on thromboembolic events, maternal mortality, and its use in women at high risk of PPH.
